title: In 1954 a group waited for a flying saucer to save them from the end of the world

cover.alt: In a 1950s living room at night, four people sit on a sofa staring hopefully at two wall clocks just before midnight, while a flying saucer glows in the window behind them.

body: In 1954 **Dorothy Martin**, of Oak Park near Chicago, said that beings from the planet Clarion were sending her messages through automatic writing: a great flood would come before dawn on 21 December, and a flying saucer would rescue the believers at midnight. The psychologists **Leon Festinger**, **Henry Riecken** and **Stanley Schachter** and their hired observers joined the group without saying who they were. When midnight passed and nothing came, a new message arrived at about 4.45 a.m.: the group's faith had saved the world. In their 1956 book *When Prophecy Fails*, which gives everyone false names, the authors reported that the believers then turned to the press to spread the word, and the case fed Festinger's theory of cognitive dissonance. A recent study of the researchers' own archives questions parts of their account, arguing that the observers influenced the group and that it was seeking converts before the failure.

slides.alt: A 1950s living room with spotted wallpaper and a floor lamp. Dorothy Martin, a grey-haired woman in a blue dress, writes on a pad at a table with her eyes closed while blue signal waves ripple above her.
slides.caption: Oak Park, near Chicago, 1954. Dorothy Martin takes dictation, by automatic writing, from the planet Clarion.

bubbles.text: They say a great flood is coming. Before dawn on 21 December.
bubbles.speaker: Dorothy Martin

slides.alt: A flying saucer with glowing portholes hovers in a starry sky, beaming green light down on four people who gaze up at it.
slides.caption: The good news: a flying saucer will collect the faithful at midnight on the 20th. Everyone else can swim.

slides.alt: Three men in dark suits, one in a fedora, stand in the living room smiling politely, each holding a little notepad.
slides.caption: Three psychologists from Minnesota join the group, pretending to believe. They want to see what happens when it fails.

bubbles.text: Just taking a few... spiritual notes.
bubbles.speaker: A psychologist

slides.alt: Night. A bald man holding wire-cutters steps towards a startled younger man in a suit; a few metal buttons and clasps lie on the floor. The clock reads 11.35.
slides.caption: 11.35 p.m. on the 20th. All metal must come off before the flight. A psychologist admits his trousers have a zip.

slides.alt: Four people sit in a row on a sofa, coats ready, smiling expectantly. Two wall clocks above them disagree: one says 11.59, the other 12.09.
slides.caption: Midnight approaches. There are two clocks, about ten minutes apart. The group goes with the slow one.

bubbles.text: And not a plan has gone astray!
bubbles.speaker: Dorothy Martin

slides.alt: The same four on the sofa, now drooping and worried. The slow clock says 12.05. Nothing is in the window.
slides.caption: 12.05 by the slow clock. No spaceman, no saucer. At 12.30 there's a knock: just some boys.

slides.alt: Dorothy Martin writes at the table, eyes shut, grinning. A man throws his arms up in joy and a woman laughs. The clock reads 4.45.
slides.caption: 4.45 a.m. A new message: the little group has spread so much light that God has saved the world.

slides.alt: Daylight. Dorothy Martin shouts into a black telephone. Behind a bathroom door left ajar, a man in a suit scribbles in a notepad.
slides.caption: Then they ring the newspapers. In the bathroom, the observers take turns writing it all down.

bubbles.text: It's the first time I've ever called them. I've never had anything to tell them before!
bubbles.speaker: Dorothy Martin

slides.question: According to the psychologists’ 1956 book, When Prophecy Fails, how did the group explain the failed flood?
options: Their faith had saved the world
slides.explanation: At about 4.45 a.m. Dorothy Martin received a message that the group had spread so much light that God had saved the world from destruction.

source.label: Festinger, Riecken and Schachter, When Prophecy Fails (1956)
